mcqs.question: Why does `isCheckmate` call `getLegalMoves` (which already filters out self-check moves) rather than `getCandidateMoves` (raw geometry) when looking for an escape?
options: Because getCandidateMoves is slower to compute than getLegalMoves
Because using raw candidate moves could report an 'escape' that's actually illegal — one that leaves the king in check — producing a false negative for checkmate
Because getLegalMoves is the only method that updates the board's move counter
Because getCandidateMoves does not exist for the King piece
mcqs.explanation: If isCheckmate checked raw candidate moves, it could find a move that looks like an escape geometrically but actually still leaves the king in check (illegal) — wrongly concluding the position isn't checkmate. getLegalMoves already applies the self-check filter, so any move found there is a genuine escape. Speed isn't the reason, no move counter is involved, and King has candidate moves like every other piece.

mcqs.question: Why is the self-check validation for a candidate move performed on a scratch copy of the board rather than the live game board?
options: Because the live board object is read-only in this design
Because scratch copies are required for the game to support two players
Because testing on a copy avoids ever leaving the authoritative game state corrupted if the move turns out to be illegal or if reverting it is incomplete
Because it makes candidate move generation faster
mcqs.explanation: Using a scratch copy (or an equivalent clean-revert mechanism) means an illegal move never has a chance to leave the real game state in a half-reverted, inconsistent condition — the live board is only ever updated once a move is confirmed legal. The live board isn't inherently read-only, two-player support is unrelated, and this doesn't affect generation speed.

mcqs.question: What's the main risk of testing self-check by mutating the live board directly and manually moving pieces back afterward?
options: It uses more memory than a scratch-copy approach
It's slower than using the Command pattern's undo
It prevents the game from ever detecting checkmate
A missed edge case in the manual revert (a captured piece, an en passant side effect, a castled rook) leaves the authoritative game state corrupted in a way that's hard to detect until later
mcqs.explanation: Manual reverts are error-prone precisely because chess moves can have side effects beyond a single piece's position — missing any of them during an ad hoc revert corrupts live game state silently. This isn't primarily a memory or speed concern, and it doesn't prevent checkmate detection specifically — it corrupts the broader game state that checkmate detection (and everything else) relies on.

mcqs.question: Why does per-piece polymorphic `getCandidateMoves()` scale better than one central switch-based move engine as chess variants or new piece types are added?
options: Because a switch-based engine requires editing existing, already-large code for every new piece type, while polymorphism adds a new independent subclass with no changes to existing pieces
Because polymorphism executes faster than a switch statement in every language
Because a switch statement cannot express diagonal movement
Because Board would otherwise be unable to store more than six piece types
mcqs.explanation: Switch-based engines require editing shared, already-large code for every new piece type; polymorphism instead adds one new independent subclass with zero changes to existing pieces. Execution speed isn't the deciding factor here, a switch statement can express diagonal movement just fine, and Board's storage isn't limited to six piece types.
